title: Reaching out for honest feedback on your game before you invest a lot of time and effort in to it is the best thing you can do early on.
author: jaykrown
selftext: I think we all have an obligation to help each other by spending even a tiny amount of time commenting and giving feedback on other's ideas. These full GTA and Minecraft clones are getting out of hand at this point.

comments.author: Tritonwolf
comments.body:
Valid point but there is an argument to be made for the exact opposite. Negative feedback at an early stage, or any feedback, can also dissuade you from an idea. Sometimes ideas are not understood at first and it may take some time for you to realize that you have something before anyone else does.

I can’t imagine how many good ideas could have been had it not been for judgmental voices that just couldn’t see something someone else did. 

History is littered with cases of people ignoring naysayers and changing the world

replies.author: CC_NHS
replies.body:
The fear of someone stealing their idea has always been a failure of solo devs starting out for as long as I have been in game dev. 

People tend to want to build their own vision, not yours, those that steal ideas are trying to just make quick cash will be stealing ideas that have proven success (hence how game clones pop up after every indie success) stealing ideas from a few sentences off Reddit is unlikely to be remotely how you intended it to be in your own mind anyway and likely not competing. And on the topic of not competing, it is better to not consider Redditors as the competition anyway, actual shipped products are the competition, and most games even if they are stolen ideas are not likely to finish.

  
tldr: if you want to finish a game, it will need as many eyes on it as you can possibly get as soon as you have something to show, and most people are not going to care about your idea.

replies.author: jaykrown
replies.body: Yea I think there's a growing delusion. The idea that if someone works really hard on a game idea using an LLM for assistance before they tell anyone about it, then when they release it they'll be a millionaire with thousands of sales. I don't think there's ever been something that's actually worked that way, and we're beginning to see clearly the value of community and history.

replies.author: LazyAp3
replies.body: I was specifically talking about idea validation, i didnt say anything about prototyping/showcases or whatever marketing you have in mind, im also a huge advocat for early playtesting and feedback driven design changes, but just dumping your ideas into the current vulture culture might not be the right move since we are already heading into the direction where your creative input and gamefeel will be the only unique selling points with how fast you can pump out decent looking working games nowadays

replies.author: CC_NHS
replies.body:
yeah my reply used 2nd person tense as if It was all directed at you, my reply was more to the general point of the idea theft that you raised rather than 'your' idea being stolen :)

getting actual validation from an idea is also quite a different thing now too, you used the term vulture culture there, and I am not sure if you mean people swoop in and steal, or just general kinda desperate behaviours. but I noticed people putting their ideas out now get far more negative replies in general and that is quite an interesting thing, I think it's a combination of people getting lazier with AI, and because AI can put out a prototype of your idea, that ideas without demonstrating are even less valuable now.

  
I rambled again, it's just what I do.

comments.author: UnderStrangeStars
comments.body:
I'm a non AI developer who comes here to try and help new developers pursue their interests.

When I review some games, it often feels like I've spent more time reviewing the game than the creator. Like they just vibed a few prompts (if that), spent no time refining / fixing anything .. and then just go blast it out like a slop grenade. Then at the first sign of valid feedback they say "well I just started it, you just hate AI, you're missing the potential" or my favorite "I'm going to do that at the end" and the \_that\_ they're describing is the core game loop that makes up 80% of the game.

I feel like people submitting their work for review should be under some obligation to respect others' time.

comments.author: Backroadsgaming
comments.body:
Absolutely agree, I think a lot of devs find it hard to take criticism of their "baby".  When I first started doing schooling for game design I had that same mind set, but now realize that negative feedback is actually better than positive. Is itndown heartening Absolutely but it helps you grow as swell as helping your game. 

I do notice though that a lot of people are asking for testers but dont test others games.

As solo devs, especially those with an extremely tight or non existent budget, free play tests are hard to come by (meaning getting people to test). I think anyone asking for play tests should also be testing others games especially the free one I understand it takes some of your time, but it does a multitude of things to help this industry. Both with and without ai.

replies.author: jaykrown
replies.body: Yea I think a lot of people using AI to help create their game idea aren't realizing that QA is an actual paid job. It's a privilege to have players that who leave feedback or mention issues they had. Negative feedback can be very valuable if interpreted correctly.
